text: The Operating Systems course was a rough start for me as a beginner juggling full‑time work, but the forums helped when I was stuck on process scheduling; I barely passed because feedback felt late, and the software stack got smoother once I learned the basics.

I liked Dr. Chen, but the grading felt rough and uneven week to week. Still, the pacing kept me engaged despite my full-time job, and I barely missed any lectures—great for someone juggling study time, though feedback often came too late for real help.

OS had its ups and downs. with a full-time job, i barely had time to breathe, and the organization felt messy—deadlines drifting, notes scattered across forums and slides that didn’t always sync. dr. chen’s feedback was clear enough to trust my grade, but the few assessments mattered a lot, and the help from peers outpaced staff, especially during office hours where i asked about a memory management question and got a concrete pointer to the forum thread.

Taking Cyber Security Basics mostly felt like trudging through recordings and slide notes, since I relied on those far more than live lectures and still ended up with mixed feelings about my grade. It’s a mid-program core intro that starts fairly accessible but ramps up sharply, and by week four I realized the assessment load was more report-heavy and time-consuming than I expected, which didn’t help when deadlines stacked on top of each other. The tooling was the real drag—an occasional platform hiccup would push a deadline by a day, and when that happens you feel all the pressure; email support was slow enough that I got frustrated right as I needed clarity. I did OK on the fairly fair exam structure, but the fatigue from constant writing and the long-form reports made the whole thing exhausting, especially during the big week where the mock incident-response report loomed. One memorable moment was the week of the final project, when I finally understood how the grading quirks worked—yet I still walked away with that “I could have studied more” ache. I’d only recommend it if you know you can prep well in advance and tolerate the rough tooling and pacing.

I took Linear Algebra mainly out of curiosity, not because I love the idea of proofs, and that tempered my experience. The platform quirks sometimes made quick tasks feel like a mini obstacle course, especially when a bug in the submission portal stalled a deadline I wasn’t expecting, which didn’t help my mood. I used the materials selectively—reading the notes when I needed a refresher for a project, and skimming lectures otherwise—and I found the deadlines stacked up in a way that left me tired and resigned. The project-heavy setup and some slow, detailed grading comments from TAs made the process feel heavier than it needed to be, and I remember one office-hour hangout where I left with more questions than answers. Overall, it was useful, but I didn’t enjoy it as a course.

Calculus II in the first semester already felt like a sprint, and the lecturer didn’t help with the pace—the talks were dry and it was hard to stay engaged, especially when many lectures were just slides with a voiceover. I mostly relied on the recordings and my notes, since the live sessions didn’t land the concepts clearly, and the math felt heavier than I expected for an advanced elective. The project-heavy setup with big exams kept me on my toes, and group work helped a bit when my teammates pulled their weight, though timing the milestones was a pain. A concrete annoyance: the ramp-up starts accessible but then shoots up quickly, so I spent a lot of late nights trying to catch up before the next deadline. Overall, I’m in the C range and still unsure how much it reflects my actual understanding.

I took Cyber Security Basics because it was required for my degree, and I kept up with nearly every lecture, though the material felt dry in the recorded sessions. The LMS and submission flow are smooth, but I remember an early confusion about threat models that shaped how I approached the rest of the term. The forums helped at times, but some replies felt dismissive, and I’d only recommend it if you come in with a solid preparation.

I slogged through Database Systems with Prof. Alvarez, and that mid-semester crunch left me tracking every late-night timestamp like a scavenger hunt. The workload felt way heavier than I expected, especially with the report-heavy tasks that ate into study time for other demanding courses, and the software stack started rough but eventually calmed down. I’d say the course lands somewhere between “solid B, given I was juggling a full-time job” and “don’t rely on it if you want easy wins.” The lecturer was clearly capable and showed up with real-world chops, but the clarity sometimes felt rough—slides and explanations didn’t always line up, and I fell behind while trying to squeeze study time around deadlines. The software stack started rough at first and then settled into something workable, and office hours were a rescue when I got stuck on a debugging snag. Most work was solo, which fit my pace, though it did make the prerequisite feel heavier than advertised; I wouldn’t take it again, but it did push me enough to keep going.

Calculus II felt useful but not enjoyable, especially since I’m juggling a full-time job and only get a few evenings to study. The conceptual explanations were solid, but the examples were thin, and getting the tool setup going for the coding/plotting parts took more effort than the learning payoff. I relied mostly on recordings and notes, and the feedback varied a lot by assignment, which made planning my few study slots feel like guesswork.

Starting with a general verdict, I’ll say I learned something but it wasn’t smooth sailing. As a new student in the discipline, I found the workload in Computer Networks to be a mixed bag: the setup for tools and the constant bit of ambiguity in instructions left a lot to interpretation, and I barely passed after wrestling with most of the term while juggling another hard class. Office hours saved me more than once—tiny clarifications about the project and a quick diff on the lab code helped me see where I went wrong—though the collaboration expectations still felt unclear and the forum discussions could be slow to respond. The plus side is that I needed this for my specialization, and the topics did click when I could focus during those late-night debugging sessions.

The OS course was fine for what it is, though the first complaint I had sticks with me: I felt the lectures moved quickly during mid-semester and I had to hustle to keep up while juggling a full-time job. Still, the instructor’s lectures were clear and the pacing wasn’t terrible, especially once I started attending almost every session. I leaned on office hours a lot—they felt like the real rescue when a tricky topic popped up and the explanations finally clicked. The workload leaned toward solo work, which fit my schedule, and the prerequisites built on what was assumed without too many surprises, though the midterm format was a bit quirky and caught me off guard. Overall, it’s workable and practical, even if I won’t miss the last-minute cram sessions.

I took Operating Systems with a full-time job, so I kept up with nearly every lecture but still felt rusty and a bit tired by week three. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which helped, but the feedback quality varied a lot by assignment, and sometimes I left a week with more questions than notes. The instructor’s delivery felt uneven week to week, which didn’t help my momentum, though I appreciated the policies overall and the academic support hours—that accountability line is fine even if communication sometimes felt sloppy. A memory that sticks is that one midterm week when the questions finally clicked after I re-read a congested diagram, even as I doubted my pace. Overall, I’m glad I stuck with it, but I’m not sold on the pacing.

Machine Learning at mid-program was rough mid-term; the grading felt opaque while TAs were helpful. I barely scraped by after a heavy term, juggling quick feedback and a long report, with the material oddly practical yet not enjoyable.

I signed up for Linear Algebra in my first semester and spent more time worrying about the curve than the actual ideas, which is not how I wanted to start the program. Dr. Singh is clearly capable, but the delivery felt uneven week to week, and I often left lectures with more questions than answers, even after rewatching the same例 playlists on the LMS. The course works better if you have a study group, so I leaned on two classmates to parse proofs and the few quick problem sets that actually made sense, though the online submission flow was smooth and the feedback whenever it arrived came fast, it was usually just a line or two explaining the answer rather than the intuition I needed. I focused on it as my main course that term, juggling another hard class, and I did learn a lot, but I also disliked the sense that important nuances slipped through the cracks in real time. I occasionally checked forums and office hours for clarifications on matrix diagonalization, but the TA visits felt brief and I still felt like I was guessing during the midterm. Not sure whether I’d recommend it, but I don’t regret the effort.

I took Database Systems in my last semester because it fit my schedule more than my interests, and as a returning student I felt rusty but the basics came back enough to keep up. The platform and submission flow were smooth, but the examples felt thin and the move from accessible prerequisites to sharp ramp-up was jarring. I remember one late-night assignment that hinged on a tricky query plan, and it didn’t help that collaboration expectations were unclear.

I’m a returning student who felt a little rusty, and Cyber Security Basics fit the summer term with its compressed pacing, but the deadlines stacked up and I often felt rushed. I used the recorded lectures as needed; they’re useful but dry, and the early weeks start accessible yet ramp up sharply, so I spent more time on the short evening study blocks than I expected. The project on threat modeling helped, but feedback came sparse and late, so I wasn’t sure I was on the right track until it mattered.

Calculus II with Prof. Cohen felt like a necessary stepping stone for the specialization, and I’m glad I took it last semester while juggling two other demanding courses. I remember hitting a wall early on with a tricky integration by parts chain, and that confusion kind of set the tone for the term; after that initial stumble, the semester dragged but I did end up building a workable intuition, even if I can’t point to a single standout moment in class. The slides were serviceable, not memorable, and I appreciated that the quick feedback on quizzes came in fast, but the explanations were often thin, which left me flipping back to the notes more than I’d like. Administrative messaging was a bit sloppy at times, but the policies themselves were fine, and the prerequisites clearly built well on what we were supposed to know. The assessment felt fair yet exhausting, and I felt like I could do okay if I kept grinding through the problem sets, though I won’t pretend it was painless. If you’re balancing a heavier load and chasing a degree milestone, you’ll get through it, but I’m still not sure I’d actively recommend it without caveats.

This summer class moved fast, and I started engaged but attendance faded as the weeks packed in. I’m juggling a full-time job, so the peer discussions helped more than the official materials, and I felt the grading didn’t match what we covered in lectures. The feedback came late, and I wished those quick, concrete notes happened earlier.

Data Structures with Prof. Rios was required for my degree, and I mostly relied on recordings and notes since attendance felt optional. The course pushed my problem-solving, and the curve bumped my grade to an A, but setup for the tools took more effort than the payoff. Office hours saved me once after a tricky recursion question; that chat was the clearest fix I remember.

Calculus II felt relevant enough, but I dragged through most of it with wavering motivation and barely squeaked by, especially since the deadlines piled up in my last semester. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, and I could handle the proofs, but tooling setup and a few grading quirks (like the weekly quizzes) were frustrating and sucked up time I didn’t have. Most peers helped each other more than staff did, and a memorable week around the midterms showed how inconsistent motivation can ruin momentum.

So I ended up making Cyber Security Basics with Prof. Rios my main focus this term, and I’ll be honest: the first thing that stuck was how clear the lectures were and how the pace felt reasonable most days, which helped since I’m juggling a full-time job. I have a strong coding background but weak theory, so I kept comparing it to the easier prerequisite and it did feel more accessible than I expected, though I still wasn’t sure if I was actually grasping the theory parts or just patching together solutions. Peer interaction helped a lot; the few study group sessions we tried really saved me on the weeks with tough deadlines, and it made the collaboration structure feel like it mattered more than lectures alone. Support-wise, office hours were sometimes sparse and came late, but when I did bring in a concrete problem, the response felt like a rescue, so those moments were crucial. The timing of feedback was a problem for me—feedback felt sparse until it was too late to fix the next assignment—so I ended up doubting my understanding even though I was coding through the tasks. In the end, the course still worked better with a study group than solo, and I kept managing it alongside work, but that late feedback loop left a lingering question about my grade.

Starting in Computer Networks, I leaned on recordings and notes a lot in the first semester, and the material felt solid but the lectures left enough ambiguity that I had to rely on the slides from Prof. Rios. The project-heavy setup with high-stakes exams pushed me to collaborate, but I occasionally felt the instructions left too much interpretation, and the prereqs seemed a bit meant for more background than advertised. Still, the practical work and the way group dynamics can click when the team functions well kept me engaged, even if I wouldn’t take it again.

Data Structures with Dr. Miller felt like a doorway I kept peeking through rather than stepping into. I’m new to the discipline, and I learned the basics mostly by using the materials only when I needed them, fitting study into short evening sessions between other obligations. The office hours were a lifeline—someone finally explained pointers in a way that clicked, though I wish the feedback on assignments came a bit sooner to help with the next week’s work. The prerequisite feel of “you should know more” clashes with what’s advertised, and the assessment mix didn’t always line up with what we covered in lectures. One memorable week was that mid-semester data-structure project deadline that quietly sneaked up, and I’m still surprised by how I remembered that. Overall, I’d still recommend it to others exploring the field, even if it’s a rough fit at times.

Dr. Singh’s lectures in the Machine Learning course were clear and the pacing mostly kept on track, which helped given I needed it for a specialization. I started off engaged, but my attendance drifted mid‑semester as deadlines stacked up and the platform quirks caused extra stress; feedback often arrived too late to help fix things before the next task. The course works best if you’re in a study group, and I’ll remember that one week’s exam as a tough scramble more than the steady guidance.

Calculus II left me exhausted and unenthused, despite some solid conceptual explanations. The grading rubric felt vague, platform quirks added stress, but office hours救ed me enough to finish a mid‑term. I’d wouldn’t take it again, though it helped somewhat.

Overall I left Calculus II feeling like the course was useful but not enjoyable, especially given how busy I am with a full-time job and multiple demanding classes. I struggled to keep up during mid-semester crunches, and the feedback curves felt sparse until it was too late to fix my approach for the next exam. Peer discussion helped more than the official materials, and I relied on a few fellow students to walk me through a tricky integration technique we saw on the midterm. The tooling setup for assignments was frustrating to get running, and when I emailed Prof. Rios for quick clarification, the reply time was slow around deadlines. Still, I can see the relevance of the topics, even if the experience left me frustrated rather than energized.

Data Structures with Prof. Rios was a mid-program core that I took because it’s required, and the pacing in lectures was clear enough to follow, though I barely passed after a rough patch midterm. Tooling was decent, and the online editor helped me keep up, but I noticed feedback on assignments varied a lot in usefulness; for example, one project critique was sharp and specific while another felt generic. I found it helps if you already know adjacent material and don’t push the time pressure too hard, since support from staff often felt thinner than students helping each other.

I took Machine Learning as part of the required track because I’d heard it would be useful for industry work, and Prof. Alvarez is clearly capable, even if I’m new to the discipline and still learning the basics. The course is organized enough that I didn’t feel totally lost week to week, and the slides are serviceable for a quick recap, though they’re not particularly memorable, so I relied more on the problem sets to ground what we discussed. There aren’t many assessments, but each one feels weighty, which adds a constant edge of pressure—the kind where you want to get it right on the first try. The platform quirks sometimes create avoidable stress, like odd submission windows or scattered feedback notifications, which didn’t help my focus when I needed it most. I found the collaboration structure works best if you have a study group; alone, I felt adrift figuring out how to connect theory to the coding tasks. One concrete moment I still think about is the capstone-style project where a small error in feature scaling sent our model performance spiraling, a reminder that the basics matter a lot, even if the course tries to be fair. Would not take it again, even though it helped, judging it against my expectations rather than another course.

Midway through the semester, I’ve found Computer Networks surprisingly usable in practice, especially since the tooling and simulators I use at work line up with the concepts Dr. Chen covers. The course moves quickly enough that I wish the communication from the admin side was a bit clearer, but the support you actually get from fellow students is solid—people pipe up with quick explanations in the chat and share shortcuts for the labs. It starts approachable but ramps up fast, which feels like it mirrors a real industry leap from the easier prerequisite, and the assignments with frequent deadlines keep me on my toes. I’d take it again only if I already had a handle on time management, because I’d rather not juggle the chaos of deadlines, but I can’t deny it helped my day-to-day work a bit.

This first semester in ML with Dr. Park dragged a bit, especially when tooling hiccups pushed deadlines and late feedback left me scrambling. Group work helped when my team clicked, but the midterm crunch and uneven pacing left me barely passing and remembering that one tricky week-long assignment.

Last semester, I used the materials selectively, since the tooling felt neutral and messy at times; the lectures were uneven, deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, and collaboration expectations were unclear, but the content helped me link adjacent material, though I still failed.

Calculus II with Dr. Singh in the summer term was a mixed bag for me, since I tried to fit short evening sessions around another hard class and ended up feeling the pacing was too compressed. The prerequisites felt fine, and the material built on what was stated, but the report-heavy assignments were time sinks that ate into study groups I relied on to stay afloat. A concrete pain point: the instructions often left room for interpretation, so I spent more time chasing formatting quirks than actually solving problems. It does help to have a study group, though—my partner and I found we could sanity-check the weekly quizzes together, even if the grading patterns were murky. One memorable week was the exam blitz in week four, where I realized I’d underestimated the number of short-answer prompts. Overall, I’m not sure the grade mirrored my understanding, and I’m leaning toward C with some doubt about whether I truly grasped the deeper concepts.

I’m new to the discipline, and the Database Systems course under Dr. Chen felt like a rough start that slowly tightened up. The exams seemed fair enough once I saw the pattern, but the quick feedback came with a thin explanation, and the assessment mix didn’t quite map to what we covered in lectures.

I started the term barely passing, honestly; the lectures felt uneven week to week, and I’m glad I had a study group because solo I’d have floundered more. Prof. Haddad’s pace and the prerequisite gap didn’t help my weak theory, though the LMS flow kept submissions smooth. I’m still not sure I’d recommend it, but the last stretch fit my tight, full-time-work schedule.

I started the advanced ML course motivated by the specialization, but the lectures felt dry and the software stack was rough at first; attendance faded mid-semester and the feedback arrived too late to help, yet the project did push me to learn.

Machine Learning with Dr. Chen was tougher than I expected for an advanced elective, and keeping up while juggling other hard courses was brutal. The setup for tools felt like a time sink, but lectures were clear and deadlines piled up.

I signed up for Data Structures out of genuine curiosity, hoping to finally get a solid sense of how these things actually fit together, but the summer term pacing felt suffocating in short evening sessions. The lectures from Dr. Miller were solid enough, and the LMS flow was smooth, which helped when I was juggling another hard class, but the overall difficulty was higher than I expected for a “foundations” vibe, especially since I was trying to fit it around late-night study blocks. Feedback timing was a mixed bag—some weeks the TAs pointed out concrete mistakes quickly, other weeks it felt like I had to chase hints; office hours ended up being the saving grace for me, a quick rescue when the code halted at the last minute.

Data Structures with Dr. Park was my first real plunge into this field, and I stuck with it mostly because it’s required for the track. I’m new to the discipline, so some days felt like wading through fog, especially when the grading rubric seemed vague and the explanations in feedback were thin. The platform quirks didn’t help—one week the quiz platform froze, and I spent extra time just reloading, which added stress around deadlines. I remember the week of the big tree-walk assignment and the exam shift; I barely passed after struggling most of the term, and the fast score return didn’t compensate with clear guidance. Email support felt slow when I needed timely help.

Taking Computer Networks with Prof. Alvarez felt like a slog most days, because the math-heavy stuff never clicked easily and I was barely keeping up, especially when the examples were thin and the concepts felt abstract until the very end. I kept thinking the prerequisites would save me, but it still required more background than I had, so I fell behind and then scrambled to catch up right around deadlines, which didn’t exactly help my morale. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which helped a bit when I finally had the mental space to push through a late assignment, but the feedback came too late to adjust my approach meaningfully. The lectures had strong conceptual explanations and I could follow the big ideas, but the concrete examples didn’t land for me, and I’m not sure I’d say I enjoyed it even though I recognize it’s useful. My motivation to take the course was mainly that the schedule fit, not because I was obsessed with the material, so it was a practical fit rather than a passion project. Overall, the course felt useful but not enjoyable, and I’m glad I survived it without failing outright.

Calculus II was a rough ride for me, especially since the slides felt serviceable but not memorable, and the pace ramped up sharply after the early chapters. I started with decent intentions, but the mid‑semester crunch and the heavy assignment load with near-constant deadlines wore me down, and the organization of the course didn’t help—things felt scattered, like signals the lecturer assumed we’d just catch on our own. The exams were fair-ish in isolation, but the way material piled up made it feel like a trap door for anyone who spaced out even once. By the end I still had mixed feelings, like I learned enough to know I’m glad it’s over, but I can’t shake the sense I could have done better with a different setup. A small moment sticks: a single friday review that actually clicked, then we moved on to the next thing.

Database Systems with Prof. Alvarez was challenging in a good way for me as a newcomer, and I appreciated the strong conceptual explanations, even though the examples felt thin at times; the TAs were quick to help, and the main exam week with that tricky data-model question still sticks in my mind.

I signed up for Linear Algebra as an advanced elective hoping to finally feel confident about matrices, and the first thing that hit me was how time-consuming the report-heavy workload is, even though I’m juggling two other demanding courses. Dr. Miller is smart, but the pace and the way the coursework piles on—lots of forums to monitor, weekly problem sets, and a big final report—left me frustrated yet fair about what I learned. The structure mostly felt like solo work, with little peer dependency, and I ended up leaning on classmates in the forums more than the staff for quick clarifications. Still, the material did build on the prerequisites, and I’d admit the insights finally clicked after a late-night office hour where a TA walked me through an example with eigenvectors. Overall, useful but not enjoyable, and I’m not sure I’d take it again.

I came into Computer Networks with genuine curiosity, but the early pace and the software stack felt rough enough to slow me down as I tried to fit study into short evening sessions. I appreciated that the prerequisite gaps cleared up more than I expected, and the instructor kept things clear enough that I could follow along, even as I was new to the discipline. The tooling got easier after a rocky start, though the platform still threw odd quirks that left me guessing at times, and the grading often seemed out of sync with what was talked about in lectures. Overall, I still remember the project and the late-night debugging session more than anything else, and that stuck with me.

the big gripe for me was the exam structure in the intro computer networks course this summer, where it felt like the questions assumed more prior exposure than the brochure suggested, so i walked into the first midterm already on edge about what the professor would consider fair to test. prof. haddad is clearly smart, and the lectures move quickly enough that i started out engaged, but attendance faded midsemester once the pacing felt compressed and the material kept looping back to tricky edge cases that didn’t get enough practice in the weekly labs. the LMS is actually smooth, submissions went through without drama, and i appreciated that aspect more than i expected, especially since deadlines tend to come in clusters and the auto-reminder system helped keep me from totally spacing. still, the instructions sometimes left too much interpretation, like a few questions on the project that could swing either way depending on which reading you focused on, which made the collaboration part feel hazy and the team dynamic a little uncertain. i’d say i’d only recommend taking it with a bit more preparation than the intro prerequisite implied, and maybe compare it to the easier prereq i took earlier, but don’t expect it to be a breeze. the whole thing left me tired and resigned, but i’ll admit the practical parts did teach me something about segmenting packets, even if the vibe was rough.

Data Structures was doable alongside my full-time job, but setup and admin chatter slowed me down more than the lectures helped. I wish the group work was officially encouraged earlier; otherwise, late-semester turning point finally clicked, even with limited weekly study time.

I’m new to this stuff, and the Database Systems intro felt heavier and less engaging than I’d hoped, especially with the chunky report-heavy weeks; the forums helped sometimes, but the vibe there could be a bit dismissive. Professor Rios’s grading rubric never felt clear, and juggling this plus another tough class made the week of the big memory-intensive exam feel rough.

I took Cyber Security Basics because I’m genuinely curious about how defenses actually work, and I was juggling a full-time job, which made the workload feel pretty real pretty fast. The project-heavy structure kept me engaged, but I left the midterm week frazzled and crunched, not sure I could have prepared any better given the time pressure. The forums helped when I ran into setup hiccups, though some threads felt a bit dismissive rather than constructive, which didn’t help a tired student mood. I’m glad the scores came quickly, but the explanations felt thin, almost like a checklist without much context for why certain choices mattered. I ended up in a C, and I’m not sure that result actually reflects my understanding, especially since the high-stakes exams and the big project both demanded different skills. There was one week—one memorable week—where the quiz and the lab felt tightly aligned, which I appreciated, but overall the tool setup and learning payoff didn’t quite feel proportional to the effort. Would I take it again? Probably not, even though it nudged me toward real questions I still think about.

I’m in the middle of this heavy semester and took Data Structures mostly out of curiosity, not bravado, but I’m still juggling full-time work, so I felt the pace in hits and misses. The biggest snag for me was the way some instructions felt open to interpretation—like the project kickoff slides left a lot of leeway, which turned into a scramble when I realized a couple of key requirements weren’t spelled out until late. That said, Prof. Rios is solid in person, and the TAs are pretty responsive and practical when you actually reach out with a specific question; their quick feedback on a linked-list implementation saved me a lot of late-night guesswork. The course leans project-heavy with high-stakes exams, and I found that the prerequisite material landed better than I expected, almost filling some gaps I thought I’d have to slog through separately. I compared this term to another course in the same term and noticed the tooling usability is just okay for me—nothing flashy, but not a disaster either. Overall, I appreciated the genuine curiosity the topics sparked, even if the admin bits left me frustrated at times.

Cyber Security Basics with Prof. Haddad felt like a mixed bag from someone who’s basically new to the field but trying to latch onto a few solid threads. The week-to-week patchiness in instruction left me uncertain about where the core ideas were landing, even as the recordings and notes kept me afloat during a busy term. Setting up the tooling was a pain at first, and I spent more time wrestling with the software stack than I’m comfortable admitting, though it did get smoother after a while. There was one memorable week on the exam format that still sticks with me—tight, high-stakes, and somehow fair. Office hours and TAs helped, but I wish the pacing and feedback felt more consistent.

Taking Computer Networks as my main focus this term, I did okay keeping up with nearly every lecture, even though the tooling sometimes sabotaged deadlines and made weeks feel extra tense. Dr. Chen is solid and the material builds on the prerequisites, but the admin side felt a bit murky—instructions left a lot of room for interpretation, which cost me time when I was juggling another hard class. The TAs were practical and responsive, which saved me during a couple of forum threads and quick office hours that week I was staring at a confusing router simulation. The standout memory is that midterm week, when one tricky lab question tied together the whole semester and I finally clicked; still, I wish the platform hadn’t hiccuped right before submission. Overall, it’s a tough, fair run, and I learned a lot, even if a few weeks felt rough.

This last semester before graduation was a grind, but the workload actually kept me moving rather than sinking into burnout, which was a surprise for an advanced elective like Operating Systems. I came in with strong coding chops but weak theory, so the upshot was a lot of practical momentum from the projects, though the readings sometimes felt static and the lectures dry as a pun. Attendance started solid when I cared about a project deadline, then faded as the weeks wore on, and the grading comments came way later than I hoped, but when they did arrive they were detailed enough to thread the mess together. A study group helped the most; the forums were useful yet occasionally dismissive, and I remember one late-night debugging session that finally clicked after we swapped ideas, even as the whole thing wore me out.

During the summer term, Dr. Singh’s Database Systems felt doable but tight, especially juggling it with two other demanding courses. The slides were solid for catching the main ideas, but the fast feedback loop—fast scores yet fairly thin explanations—left me re-reading forum threads and popping into TA office hours to actually connect the dots. The deadlines on tooling issues made a couple of weeks feel harsher, and I’d probably only recommend it if you’re ready to put in the prep work and keep up with the forums or the TA hours.

I liked the instructor a lot, but the grading felt odd and sparse until the end. The lectures were dry, though the forums and office hours helped; I stayed solid B, juggling time and spurts of motivation, with the project deadline pattern sticking in my head.

Calculus II was fine for me mid-semester when I was juggling a heavy load and trying to fit the coding projects into a schedule. I appreciated the clear lectures and decent pacing, and the peer help was surprisingly strong—people in my study group explained the tricky chain-rule-in-disguise parts better than the TA did. I came in with strong coding chops but weaker theory, so I leaned on the practice problems and occasionally skimmed the staff notes; the tool setup and platform take more effort than the payoff, though.
